bib.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
bib.venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 23 (2022) 1-40 (arXiv v3, 16 Jun 2022; first posted 2021)

question: Can a simplified sparse mixture-of-experts layer (top-1 routing) make it practical to scale parameter count at constant FLOPs per token, with stable training and better speed-quality than dense T5?
hypothesis: Parameter count, independent of total computation performed, is a separately important axis on which to scale.
contributions: The Switch Transformer architecture, which simplifies and improves over Mixture of Experts.
Scaling properties and a benchmark against the strongly tuned T5 model with 7x+ pre-training speedups at the same FLOPS per token.
Distillation of sparse pre-trained and fine-tuned models into small dense models, preserving 30% of the quality gains with up to 99% fewer parameters.
Improved training and fine-tuning techniques: selective precision, smaller initialization scale, expert dropout.
Multilingual pre-training gains across all 101 languages over mT5-Base.
Models up to 1.6T parameters by combining data, model and expert parallelism.

method.summary: Replace the dense FFN in a T5 Transformer with a Switch FFN layer: a learned router sends each token to a single expert FFN (k=1), with a fixed expert capacity and an auxiliary load-balancing loss. Models are FLOP-matched to T5-Base/Large/XXL, pre-trained on C4 with span-corruption MLM on TPUs via Mesh-TensorFlow, then fine-tuned, distilled and tested multilingually.
method.task: Masked-language-model pre-training (T5 span corruption) on C4, then fine-tuning on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, summarization, closed-book QA, ARC, ANLI, Winogrande; multilingual pre-training on mC4

datasets.name: C4 (improved, de-duplicated within example)
datasets.split: pre-train 2^20 tokens per batch for 550k steps = 576B tokens (so repeated); validation neg log perplexity reported
datasets.source: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (Raffel et al. 2019), revised to remove intra-example duplication (Lee et al. 2021)
datasets.preprocessing: Drop 15% of tokens and replace the masked sequence with a single sentinel token

datasets.name: mC4
datasets.size: 101 languages, 107 tasks due to script variants

datasets.name: GLUE and SuperGLUE
datasets.split: validation sets; tasks blended as composite mixtures in proportion to tokens

datasets.name: CNNDM, XSum, SQuAD, ARC, Natural/Web/Trivia Questions (closed book), Winogrande, ANLI

models.name: Switch-Base
models.params: 7B (Table 9); 3,800M, 1.1B-14.7B in distillation experiments (varying experts); 7,410M in Table 8
models.architecture: T5-Base with Switch FFN at every other FFN layer (expert freq 1/2), 128 experts

models.name: Switch-Large
models.architecture: FLOP-matched to T5-Large, expert freq 1/2, 128 experts

models.name: Switch-XXL
models.architecture: FLOP-matched to T5-XXL, expert freq 1/2, 64 experts, uses model parallelism

models.name: Switch-C
models.architecture: expert-parallel only, expert freq 1 (every layer), 2048 experts

other.note: Table 9 prints no FFN_GEGLU tick for this row

models.name: MoE-Base (top-2 routing)
models.architecture: Switch-Base layout with top-2 routing, 128 experts, every other FFN

models.name: Switch-Base+
models.architecture: Switch-Base with hidden size 768 -> 896 and heads 14 -> 16, to match MoE speed

other.note: Table 1 caption says heads 14 -> 16 though T5-Base has 12 heads in Table 9

training.objective: Span-corruption masked LM (15% tokens dropped, single sentinel) plus auxiliary load-balancing loss alpha * N * sum_i f_i * P_i
training.batch_size: 2^20 (1,048,576) tokens per batch for the 550k-step protocol; 524k tokens per batch in Table 10; fine-tuning batch size 1M
training.steps: 550k pre-training (T5/Switch fine-tuning protocol); 1M for mSwitch/mT5; 100k in Table 1; fine-tuning 16k steps, evaluated every 200 steps, peak validation score reported
training.tokens: 576B total tokens (550k steps x 2^20); Switch-XXL checkpoint for multi-task: 503B tokens
training.precision: bfloat16 with the router computed in float32 (selective precision); float32 router output recast to bfloat16
training.dropout: fine-tuning: 0.1 on all layers except expert layers at 0.4 (expert dropout)
training.regularisation: Load-balancing loss alpha=1e-2 (swept 1e-1 to 1e-5 in powers of 10); input jitter noise on router (multiplicative, eps value not stated); init: truncated normal, std sqrt(s/n), s reduced 1.0 -> 0.1; capacity factor 1.0-2.0; dropped tokens (<1%) pass via residual
training.hardware: TPUv3; 32 cores for Table 1 and Fig 5; Mesh-TensorFlow
training.seeds: 3 random seeds for Table 3 (32 experts, 3.5k steps); not stated elsewhere

other.expert_capacity: (tokens per batch / number of experts) x capacity factor
other.init: truncated normal, mean 0, std sqrt(s/n), n = fan-in, values beyond 2 std resampled
other.distillation: init non-expert weights from teacher; 0.25 teacher probabilities + 0.75 ground truth label loss
other.optimizer_and_lr_not_stated: paper gives no optimizer, learning rate or schedule

metrics.name: Negative log perplexity (C4)
metrics.definition: log base e, so units are nats; higher (closer to 0) is better

metrics.name: Time to quality threshold
metrics.definition: hours to reach Neg. Log Perp. = -1.50

metrics.name: Step speedup
metrics.definition: ratio of steps baseline needs to steps model needs to reach the same quality

metrics.name: Exact match
metrics.definition: SQuAD and closed-book QA (percentage of answers exactly matching target)

metrics.name: Percent of teacher quality gain preserved
metrics.definition: percent of quality difference between Switch-Base teacher and T5-Base student recovered

eval.protocol: Single runs for most comparisons (seeds only given for Table 3); fine-tuning reports peak validation performance evaluated every 200 steps; no significance tests. Authors say further statistics are needed for the upstream/downstream relation.

availability.code: JAX code and all model checkpoints at https://github.com/google-research/t5x; TensorFlow code at https://github.com/tensorflow/mesh/blob/master/mesh_tensorflow/transformer/moe.py

evidence.quote: we pre-train with 220 (1,048,576) tokens per batch for 550k steps amounting to 576B total tokens
using a dropout rate of 0.1 for all layers except the Switch layers, which use a dropout rate of 0.4

results.claim: A 64-expert Switch-Base reaches T5-Base's quality in one-seventh the wall-clock time at equal FLOPs per example.
results.setup: Switch-Base 64 experts vs T5-Base, C4 pre-training, 32 TPUv3 cores, equal FLOPs per example (Fig 5)
results.quote: Our 64 expert Switch-Base model achieves the same quality in one-seventh the time of the T5-Base and continues to improve.
results.note: Abstract says up to 7x; Fig 5 label 7x Speedup

results.claim: On a step basis, Switch-Base 64e reaches at step 60k the quality T5-Base has at step 450k.
results.setup: Switch-Base 64 experts vs T5-Base, C4 pre-training
results.quote: which is a 7.5x speedup in terms of step time
results.note: Text reads 'achieves the same performance of the T5-Base model at step 60k at step 450k' and the sentence order is garbled in the source; the intended meaning is Switch step 60k matches T5-Base step 450k. Read the quote as printed.

results.claim: Switch-Base is 2.5x faster in wall-clock than T5-Large, which uses 3.5x more FLOPs per token.
results.setup: Switch-Base 64e vs T5-Large, C4 pre-training
results.quote: Switch-Base is still more sample efficient and yields a 2.5x speedup

results.claim: Switch-C (1.6T parameters, 2048 experts) is 4x faster to a fixed perplexity than T5-XXL at the same compute budget.
results.setup: C4 pre-training, Switch-C vs T5-XXL (T5-XXL pre-trained on easier C4 with duplicates, so gap is a lower bound)
results.quote: Switch-C Transformer variant is 4x faster to a fixed perplexity (with the same compute budget) than the T5-XXL model

results.claim: Switch-XXL beats T5-XXL on C4 neg log perplexity by 0.087 at 500k steps.
results.setup: Switch-XXL (395B) vs T5-XXL at 500k steps; T5-XXL -1.095, Switch-XXL -1.008
results.quote: with the Switch-XXL model out-performing the T5-XXL by 0.087 by 500k steps

results.claim: Switch-Base (1.0 capacity factor) trains faster and reaches the -1.50 threshold sooner than MoE-Base at every capacity factor tested.
results.setup: 128 experts, expert every other FFN, 32 TPUv3 cores; Switch-Base cf 1.0 vs MoE-Base cf 1.0
results.table: Table 1, rows Switch-Base 1.0 and MoE-Base 1.0, column Time to Quality Threshold
results.note: T5-Base did not reach threshold in 100k steps; T5-Large 131.1 hours

results.claim: Without selective precision, bfloat16 Switch-Base diverges; casting the router to float32 recovers float32 quality at near bfloat16 speed.
results.metric: neg log perplexity / examples per sec
results.setup: 32-expert Switch-Base, fixed early step count; float32 -1.718 at 1160 ex/s, selective -1.716 at 1390 ex/s
results.table: Table 2, row Switch-Base (Selective precision), column Quality

results.claim: Reducing init scale by 10x raises mean quality and cuts run-to-run std from 0.68 to 0.01.
results.setup: 32-expert Switch-Base after 3.5k steps, 3 seeds; mean -2.72 (0.1x) vs -3.60 (1.0x)
results.table: Table 3, row Switch-Base (0.1x-init), column Std. Dev. of Quality

results.claim: Expert dropout 0.4 with 0.1 elsewhere gives the best fine-tuning on GLUE (85.2) vs 84.7 at uniform dropout 0.1.
results.setup: Switch-Base pre-trained on 34B tokens of C4; see Table 4 for CNNDM, SQuAD, SuperGLUE
results.table: Table 4, row Switch-Base (d=0.1, ed=0.4), column GLUE

results.claim: Fine-tuned Switch-Base beats T5-Base on SuperGLUE by 4.4 points and Switch-Large beats T5-Large by 2.
results.setup: FLOP-matched; 550k steps pre-training at 2^20 tokens per batch; validation set; peak over evals every 200 steps
results.quote: FLOP-matched Switch variants improve by 4.4 and 2 percentage points over the T5-Base and T5-Large baselines

results.claim: Switch-Large reaches 83.0 on Winogrande XL vs 79.1 for T5-Large; Switch-Base 73.3 vs 66.6.
results.setup: Fine-tuned, validation set

results.claim: Switch models do not win on ARC: T5-Base beats Switch-Base on ARC Challenge, T5-Large beats Switch-Large on ARC Easy.
results.setup: Fine-tuned, validation set
results.table: Table 5, row Switch-Base, column ARC Chal.

results.claim: Distilling Switch-Base into T5-Base (non-expert init plus 0.75 hard/soft mix) preserves about 30% of the quality gain with about 1/20 of the parameters.
results.setup: Teacher Switch-Base 3,800M, student T5-Base 223M; -1.580 distilled vs -1.636 T5-Base vs -1.444 teacher
results.quote: By combining both techniques we preserve ≈30% of the quality gains from the larger sparse models with only ≈1/20th of the parameters.
results.note: Table 6 prints 29%; Table 7 prints 30 % for the 3.8B teacher; Table 6 caption says '100x more parameters' while text says 1/20th (3,800M/223M is about 17x)

results.claim: Compressing a 14.7B Switch by 99% still keeps 28% of the quality gain; a 1.1B teacher keeps 37% at 82% compression.
results.setup: Distilled into T5-Base 223M; pre-training neg log perplexity
results.quote: At the extreme, where we compress the model 99%, we are still able to maintain 28% of the teacher’s model quality improvement.

results.claim: Distilling a SuperGLUE-fine-tuned 7.4B Switch-Base into T5-Base reaches 76.6, preserving 30% of the gain.
results.setup: Switch-Base 7410M teacher 81.3; student 223M
results.table: Table 8, row Distilled T5-Base, column SuperGLUE
results.note: Table 8 T5-Base 74.6 and Table 5 T5-Base 75.1 differ (different protocols)

results.claim: In multilingual pre-training Switch improves on mT5-Base in all 101 languages with a mean 5x step speedup; 91% of languages get at least 4x.
results.setup: mSwitch-Base vs mT5-Base, mC4, 1M steps, FLOP-matched
results.quote: We find a mean speed-up over mT5-Base of 5x and that 91% of languages achieve at least a 4x speedup.

results.claim: Switch-XXL multi-task SQuAD validation is 89.7 vs state of the art 91.3; ANLI 65.7 vs prior best 49.4.
results.setup: Switch-XXL partially pre-trained on 503B tokens (about half of T5-XXL's), multi-task trained
results.quote: Switch XXL improves over the prior state-of-the-art to get a 65.7 accuracy versus the prior best of 49.4
results.note: SuperGLUE test sentence is garbled in source: 87.5 vs T5 89.3 vs state of the art 90.0. Section 8 says Switch-XXL SQuAD is 89.6 while Section 5.6 says 89.7.

results.claim: Closed-book QA on Switch-XXL: Natural Questions 34.4 (prior 32.8), Web Questions 41.0 (37.2), TriviaQA 47.5 (42.9).
results.setup: Switch-XXL, no Salient Span Masking, prior best T5-XXL

results.claim: Switch-C (1.6T) gets 87.7 SQuAD exact match, worse than smaller Switch-XXL at 89.6, despite similar C4 perplexity.
results.setup: Switch-C vs Switch-XXL
results.quote: the 1.6T parameter Switch-C achieves only an 87.7 exact match score in SQuAD, which compares unfavorably to 89.6 for the smaller Switch-XXL model

results.claim: Switch-XXL is sometimes unstable while Switch-C shows no instability, so Switch-XXL was not pre-trained for the full 1M steps.
results.setup: Switch-XXL (about 10x FLOPs per sequence of Switch-C), Switch-C with 2048 experts

results.claim: Router exploration: input jitter (-1.468) performs best, sampling from the softmax is worst (-1.570).
results.setup: Switch Transformer, appendix C
results.table: Table 11, row Input jitter, column Quality
results.note: Table 11 caption says 'lower is better' but the column header has the up arrow (higher is better); the values are negative log perplexity

results.claim: Experts in self-attention (Q,K,V) improve quality but diverge in bfloat16, so were not used.
results.setup: 32 experts, 524k tokens per batch, float32; Expert Attention vs Experts FF
results.table: Table 10, row Expert Attention float32, column Quality @100k Steps

results.claim: Dense models often do better than Switch at a fixed upstream perplexity on SuperGLUE in the large regime; on TriviaQA Switch may do better.
results.setup: Fig 13 scatter of C4 neg log perplexity vs downstream score, validation sets
results.note: Authors: further statistics (expensive to collect and left to future work) would be necessary to confirm.

results.claim: Models with as few as two experts improve over FLOP-matched T5-Base.
results.setup: Switch-Base with 2, 4, 8 experts vs T5-Base (Fig 12, read from figure)

limits: Switch-XXL training is sometimes unstable; stability remains unsolved for the largest models (Section 8).
Upstream perplexity gains do not always translate to downstream: Switch-C (1.6T) SQuAD 87.7 vs Switch-XXL 89.6; on SuperGLUE the dense model often does better at fixed perplexity in the large regime.
Largest-model downstream results are preliminary, from a partially pre-trained checkpoint (503B tokens), and below SOTA on SQuAD and SuperGLUE.
No optimizer, learning rate, warmup or schedule is given; most comparisons are single runs.
Speed measurements depend on implementation (Mesh-TensorFlow on TPUv3) as well as algorithm; MoE capacity 2.0 to 1.25 slowing down is called unexpected.
Baseline T5-XXL was trained on an easier, duplicated C4, so the gap to Switch-XXL is a lower bound.
Only the FFN is made sparse; expert attention was unstable in bfloat16. Language only; no other modalities.
Distillation recovers about 30% of the gain, not the full quality.

terms.definition: the number of tokens each expert computes, set by evenly dividing tokens in the batch across experts, then multiplying by a capacity factor
k = 1 routing strategy, routing a token to only a single expert
tokens routed to an expert beyond its capacity; computation is skipped and the representation passes through the residual connection
increasing the dropout rate only at the interim feed-forward computation inside each expert during fine-tuning

lineage.note: Switch simplifies top-k MoE routing to k=1 and merges the two balancing losses
MoE Transformer; source of the overflow residual handling and auxiliary loss
Dense baselines and C4 pre-training recipe

lineage.work: Scaling laws for neural language models (Kaplan et al.)
lineage.note: Adds parameter count at constant FLOPs as a fourth axis
Selective precision in line with mixed-precision strategies

lineage.work: Distilling the knowledge in a neural network (Hinton et al.)
lineage.note: Distillation; techniques follow Sanh et al. 2019 (DistilBERT)

lineage.work: Shazeer et al. 2017 claim that k>1 is needed for routing gradients
lineage.quote: Contrary to these ideas, we instead use a simplified strategy where we route to only a single expert.

lineage.work: Deduplicating training data makes language models better (Lee et al.)
GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, CNNDM, XSum, ARC, Natural Questions, WebQuestions, TriviaQA, Winogrande, ANLI

code.snippet: loss = alpha * N * sum_{i=1..N} f_i * P_i; f_i = (1/T) sum_{x in B} 1{argmax p(x) = i}; P_i = (1/T) sum_{x in B} p_i(x)
expert capacity = (tokens per batch / number of experts) x capacity factor
